params.question: The body absorbs enough iron from food each day to fully compensate for the increased demand of pregnancy without relying on stored iron.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The video explains that the gut absorbs only 1–2 mg of iron daily — barely enough to cover normal losses. In pregnancy, demand rises sharply, and the narrow absorption margin widens into a deficit that the body cannot close through absorption alone. This is why iron stores deplete and deficiency is so common in pregnancy.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The gut absorbs only 1–2 mg of iron per day, which barely covers normal daily losses of the same magnitude. In pregnancy, demand rises sharply, and this narrow absorption margin cannot keep pace. The body must draw on stored iron, often resulting in iron deficiency if reserves are inadequate.

interactions.label: A patient is advised to take iron tablets on an empty stomach with orange juice

params.question: A patient is advised to take iron tablets on an empty stomach with orange juice and to avoid tea. Which aspect of iron absorption physiology best supports this advice?

answers.text: An empty stomach allows haem iron to bypass DMT1 entirely, while tea blocks ferroportin-mediated export on the basolateral side

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haem iron enters the enterocyte intact regardless of stomach contents. The clinical advice targets non-haem iron absorption, which depends on luminal pH and reducing agents. Tea polyphenols act in the gut lumen, not on basolateral ferroportin.

answers.text: Orange juice increases hepatic transferrin synthesis, while tea degrades hephaestin on the basolateral membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vitamin C does not alter transferrin production by the liver, and tea polyphenols act in the gut lumen — not on the basolateral membrane. The relevant mechanisms operate at the luminal surface of the enterocyte.

answers.text: Gastric acid and vitamin C promote the ferric-to-ferrous iron conversion required for DMT1 uptake, while tea polyphenols inhibit non-haem iron absorption in the lumen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Non-haem iron must be reduced from Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ by duodenal cytochrome b before DMT1 can transport it into the enterocyte. Vitamin C and gastric acid facilitate this reduction, while polyphenols in tea chelate iron and reduce its availability for uptake.

answers.text: Vitamin C chelates iron and prevents its absorption, so it should be taken at a different time from iron supplements

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vitamin C actually enhances iron absorption by acting as a reducing agent that converts ferric to ferrous iron. It should be taken together with iron supplements, not separately.

overallFeedback.feedback: Non-haem iron (85–90% of dietary iron) must be converted from ferric (Fe³⁺) to ferrous (Fe²⁺) form by duodenal cytochrome b before DMT1 can transport it. Vitamin C and gastric acid promote this reduction, while tea polyphenols inhibit absorption — hence the advice to take iron with orange juice and away from tea.
Well done. As the narration states: 'That advice is physiology, not habit.' The iron supplement guidance is grounded directly in the biochemistry of non-haem iron uptake at the duodenal brush border.

params.question: The video states that serum ferritin falls before serum iron or haemoglobin changes. Why is serum ferritin the earliest laboratory marker of iron deficiency?

answers.text: Ferritin is produced only in bone marrow erythroblasts, which are the first cells to sense iron depletion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ferritin is found in hepatocytes, macrophages, and enterocytes — not exclusively in the bone marrow. Its early decline reflects depletion of the body's storage pool, not marrow-specific sensing.

answers.text: Ferritin has a shorter half-life than haemoglobin, so its plasma concentration drops more rapidly when iron intake declines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The early fall in serum ferritin is not primarily due to half-life differences. It reflects the physiological priority: the body sacrifices storage reserves to maintain the functional pool as long as possible.

answers.text: Serum ferritin directly measures free iron in the plasma, which is consumed before the storage pool

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serum ferritin does not measure free iron — it reflects intracellular iron stores. Free plasma iron is negligible; the measured transport fraction is transferrin-bound iron, which falls at a later stage.

answers.text: The body draws on the storage pool first when iron balance turns negative, and ferritin leaking into plasma reflects this decline before the transport or functional pools are compromised

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When losses exceed absorption, the body depletes ferritin and hemosiderin reserves before compromising transferrin-bound transport iron or haemoglobin production. Serum ferritin reflects intracellular stores, so it falls at the earliest stage of negative iron balance.

overallFeedback.feedback: Serum ferritin falls first because the storage pool is the body's buffer — it is consumed before transport iron or haemoglobin production is compromised. A small amount of intracellular ferritin leaks into plasma, providing a direct readout of these declining stores.
Exactly right. One nanogram per millilitre of serum ferritin corresponds to roughly 8 mg of stored body iron, making it the most direct and earliest window into declining iron reserves.

interactions.label: A patient has low serum ferritin, low serum iron, elevated TIBC, and a normal ha

params.question: A patient has low serum ferritin, low serum iron, elevated TIBC, and a normal haemoglobin level. Which stage of iron deficiency does this laboratory profile represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In stage 1, only ferritin is low. Serum iron, TIBC, and haemoglobin all remain normal because only the storage pool has been affected so far.

Correct. In stage 2, the storage pool is exhausted (low ferritin) and the transport pool is failing (low serum iron, elevated TIBC, low transferrin saturation), but haemoglobin production is not yet compromised. This is the window for intervention before frank anaemia develops.
Stage 3 requires haemoglobin to have fallen, with microcytic hypochromic red cells on the peripheral smear. This patient's haemoglobin is still normal.

In anaemia of chronic disease, TIBC is typically low or normal (not elevated), and ferritin is raised because hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration locks iron inside macrophages — the opposite ferritin pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: This profile — low ferritin, low serum iron, elevated TIBC, but normal haemoglobin — represents stage 2 (iron-deficient erythropoiesis). The storage pool is depleted and transport iron is failing, but haemoglobin has not yet fallen.
Well done. Recognising stage 2 allows early intervention before overt anaemia develops. The pattern to anchor: ferritin falls first, transport iron falls second, haemoglobin falls last.
